# Block 3 — Results: Calibration & Robustness Probes

Continues the deck after the "Metrics" slide — the method and measured results for
calibration (T9) and the four adversarial probes (T10). All numbers are measured on
SuperPOD (1×H800, NF4). Blue = JEV-9B, orange = Qwen3.5-9B.

---

## Slide 1 — T9 Calibration: the score location bias

**Temperature can't fix a location bias**

- **Observed:** JEV's 6-class toxicity-count head is biased *high* — mean predicted score 2.55 vs true mean 0.64, yet corr(gold, E[score]) = **+0.61** (real ordinal signal in the logits).
- **Why temperature fails:** `softmax(logits / T)` only widens the distribution; it cannot move the mode. The old fit railed to T≈32 and flattened everything to near-uniform (Brier → 0.83 ≈ the trivial 5/6 predictor).
- **Fix — ordinal scaling:** `softmax(logits / T + γ·i)` adds a *location* term along the score axis. Fitted **γ = −2.0** (T ≈ 0.98) by minimizing NLL.

**JEV · toxicity count — before → after (held-out fit):**

| ACC | QWK | MAE | ECE (15-bin) | Brier |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0.202 → **0.667** | 0.210 → **0.439** | 1.947 → **0.479** | 0.193 → **0.086** | 0.953 → **0.416** |

![Ordinal scaling mechanism][fig1]

*Left: temperature widens but keeps the mode. Right: the location term γ shifts the mode down (illustrative, not measured data).*

> **Speaker script:** Block 3 is about calibration — turning a model's raw probabilities into numbers we can trust. The headline is on the count task. JEV's decision head is biased high: it predicts a mean score of 2.55 when the true mean is 0.64. But the ranking is real — the expected score correlates 0.61 with the gold label. Temperature scaling can only widen the distribution; it cannot move the mode, so it flattened everything to near-uniform. That is why we added a location term, gamma times the class index. Fitting it on held-out data gives gamma equal to minus 2, which shifts the mode down. Accuracy goes from 0.20 to 0.67, QWK from 0.21 to 0.44, and Brier from 0.95 to 0.42. The signal was in the logits all along; only the head's location was wrong.

---

## Slide 2 — T9 Results: four tasks

**JEV ranks best on every task; Qwen's binaries need a learned threshold**

- **SMS spam (628):** JEV ACC 0.946, AUC 0.967. Qwen raw ACC 0.312 (answers "yes" 99% of the time) → **0.830 after Platt**; AUC 0.857.
- **Phishing (797, length-matched):** JEV AUC **0.914**, ACC 0.625 → **0.838**. Qwen AUC **0.713**, ACC 0.566 → 0.659. Length-matching removed a format confound that had inflated both models to AUC ≈ 1.0.
- **Toxicity binary (1,016):** JEV ACC 0.816 → **0.856**, AUC 0.928. Qwen ACC 0.582 → 0.646, AUC 0.699.
- **Toxicity count (1,016):** JEV ACC 0.202 → **0.667**, QWK 0.210 → **0.439**. Qwen degenerates to the class prior (QWK = 0; predicts all-"0").

| Task (n) | Model | ACC raw→cal | ECE raw→cal | Brier raw→cal | AUC / QWK |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SMS spam (628) | JEV | 0.946→0.946 | 0.162→0.026 | 0.075→0.046 | AUC 0.967 |
| SMS spam (628) | Qwen | 0.312→0.830 | 0.362→0.036 | 0.293→0.126 | AUC 0.857 |
| Phishing (797) | JEV | 0.625→0.838 | 0.159→0.037 | 0.217→0.118 | AUC 0.914 |
| Phishing (797) | Qwen | 0.566→0.659 | 0.112→0.037 | 0.230→0.214 | AUC 0.713 |
| Toxicity binary (1,016) | JEV | 0.816→0.856 | 0.075→0.026 | 0.129→0.106 | AUC 0.928 |
| Toxicity binary (1,016) | Qwen | 0.582→0.646 | 0.014→0.025 | 0.239→0.221 | AUC 0.699 |
| Toxicity count (1,016) | JEV | 0.202→0.667 | 0.193→0.086 | 0.953→0.416 | QWK 0.210→0.439 |
| Toxicity count (1,016) | Qwen | 0.633→0.661 | 0.237→0.023 | 0.626→0.539 | QWK 0.008→0.000 |

![Reliability diagrams][fig2]

*Reliability diagrams (raw vs held-out recalibration) for both models across all four tasks. The phishing panel uses the length-matched rebuild.*

> **Speaker script:** This slide is the main comparison across the four tasks, and two patterns stand out. First, JEV has the best ranking everywhere — AUC 0.97 on SMS, 0.91 on phishing, 0.93 on binary toxicity. Second, Qwen's binary tasks have decent ranking but a broken raw threshold: it answers "yes" almost all the time. On SMS it is only 0.31 raw, but after Platt scaling, which learns a threshold, it is 0.83. That is accuracy after learning a threshold, not native accuracy — that distinction matters. On the count task Qwen collapses to the class prior, with QWK zero. The phishing panel is new: we rebuilt it because the original corpus was separable by length alone. After length-matching, both models drop from a perfect 1.0 to a realistic 0.91 and 0.71, so the task now actually separates them.

## Slide 3 — T10 Robustness: four adversarial probes

**JEV ignores surface form; Qwen does not**

- **Setup:** 4 probes × 200 pairs — option renaming, option-order permutation, abstain removal, prompt injection.
- **JEV** flips ≤ 5% on every surface-form probe; probability TV distance ≤ 0.035.
- **Qwen** flips 11.5% on renaming and 23.5% on order permutation; forced-choice accuracy after removing "unsure" is 0.46 vs JEV's 0.89.
- **Interpretation:** Qwen's choices track *how options are presented*, not the text content.

![T10 probe results][fig3]

*Left: decision flip rate under surface-form perturbations. Right: forced-choice accuracy once the abstain option is removed.*

> **Speaker script:** T10 probes robustness to surface form. We generate four probes, two hundred pairs each. JEV flips at most five percent on any of them, with tiny probability movement. Qwen is much more sensitive: eleven and a half percent flip when we rename the options, twenty-three and a half percent when we reverse their order, and its forced-choice accuracy after removing "unsure" is 0.46 against JEV's 0.89. The interpretation is that Qwen's choices track how the options are presented, not what the text says. Prompt injection is less informative here because Qwen already says yes ninety-five percent of the time — a ceiling effect.

---

## Slide 4 — Latency & takeaways

**Latency & takeaways**

- **Latency (in-process, NF4, 1×H800):** JEV 161 ms mean (p50 142, p95 215) vs Qwen 156 ms (p50 145, p95 183) — comparable.
- **1 ·** JEV-9B is the stronger model end-to-end — best AUC on every task.
- **2 ·** Its only flaw was a decision-head *location* bias on the count task, fixed by ordinal scaling (γ = −2.0).
- **3 ·** Qwen has usable ranking on the binary tasks but a broken raw threshold; Platt recovers accuracy. Its toxicity count has no ordinal signal (QWK = 0).
- **4 ·** Calibration fixes *confidence* and the *threshold*, not *ranking* — report raw and recalibrated, with CIs.

![Latency comparison][fig4]

*Per-item latency is comparable; note this is in-process batch inference, not HTTP end-to-end.*

> **Speaker script:** Latency is comparable — about 160 milliseconds per item for both models, on one H800 with four-bit weights. Now the takeaways. JEV is the stronger model end to end, with the best AUC on every task. Its one flaw was a location bias on the count head, which we fixed at report time. Qwen has usable ranking but needs a learned threshold, and its count task has no ordinal signal at all. And the framing that runs through the whole deck: calibration fixes confidence and the decision threshold, not ranking — so we always report raw and recalibrated numbers side by side.

---

### Data note

Four tasks, matching the deck's "Data Selection": SMS spam (628 = SMS+Enron), phishing
(797, length-matched), toxicity binary (1,016, Jigsaw `toxic` label), toxicity count
(1,016, Jigsaw subtype sum). The phishing task was rebuilt because the original corpus
(CEAS 2008) was trivially separable by email length/format (AUC ≈ 1.0 for both models);
the rebuild balances classes and matches length (AUC(length) ≈ 0.5). Toxicity binary and
count share the same 1,016 comments, so they are aligned ground truth, not independent
samples.
